claims.text: High-entropy alloys were initially designed as single-phase concentrated solid solutions.
The initial alloy is a pristine single-phase solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial alloy has stable, continuous dislocation pathways.
Demanding mechanical loading causes localized chemical segregation and/or nanoscale secondary-phase formation in the nominally single-phase alloy.
The load-induced segregation or secondary phases occur at grain boundaries or within the matrix.
Mechanical loading accelerates local chemical inhomogeneity and alters dislocation pathways.
Dislocation behavior and defect activity can influence the mechanical properties and toughness of HEAs.
Local chemical inhomogeneity and altered dislocation pathways nucleate brittle nanoscale domains.
Brittle nanoscale domains interrupt the alloy's initially uniform plastic flow.
Loss of a continuous ductile matrix reduces damage tolerance and initiates brittle fracture.
Loaded specimens will contain segregated phases or ordered nanoscale domains correlated with strain-localization zones.
Loaded specimens will have lower fracture toughness than unaltered baseline specimens.
Loading will change fracture morphology from ductile dimples to brittle cleavage features.
The unloaded baseline has continuous strain hardening and high damage tolerance.
The proposed embrittlement occurs when strain rate, cyclic or sustained stress, and temperature variation reach thresholds that trigger local phase instability.
Below the phase-instability thresholds, the alloy maintains its toughness.
Identical unloaded specimens provide the control for specimens exposed to high strain rate, cyclic loading, and temperature cycling.
The hypothesis is falsified if loaded specimens show neither segregation or secondary-phase formation nor a loss of toughness or ductile fracture morphology relative to the baseline.
